checks.label: One radian is the measure of a central angle of a circle that intercepts an arc equal in length to the radius of that circle: at every size the handle can set, the arm turned to exactly 1 radian ends where the first rod ends, the rod lies on the drawn edge, its length measured along the edge equals the drawn radius, the wedge reads 1 radian and the readout 1.00 radians = 57.3°

The arc length produced by any given angle also has a constant relation to the radius, regardless of the length of the radius: with the arm held at 0.5, 1, 2, π and 5 radians, at every size from the smallest circle to the largest, the rod laid from the start to the arm, measured along the drawn edge and divided by the drawn radius, gives the same count, the angle in radians, and the readout does not change

Degree measure and radian measure are related by the equation 360° = 2π radians, or 180° = π radians: on the full-wrap screen the rod laid all the way round makes six whole rods and 0.28 of a seventh, ends back where it started, and the readout reads 6.28 radians = 360.0°; at the half turn it reads 3.14 radians = 180.0° with the arm pointing straight left

One radian is 180° ÷ π = 57.3°, a little under a sixth of the circle, not the whole circle: the shaded slice spans exactly the first rod and is labelled 57.3°, six such slices fall short of a full turn and seven pass it
The bendy rod does not stretch: at every moment of the first screen's lift and bend it is one radius long, it starts lying on the arm and it ends lying round the edge from where the arm starts

An angle with no degree sign is in radians, and the two can be far apart: the dashed arm turned 10 radians, measured off the drawing, ends at 213.0°, left of the centre and below it, after 1.59 turns, its across distance over the radius is cos 10 = −0.839, and the solid arm at 10° gives cos 10° = 0.985

Each radian of angle holds one radius of edge, so the arc is s = rθ: at every turn of the winch drum from 0.1 to 3 radians, the wire wound on, measured along the drawn edge, and the hook's rise measured off the drawing both equal the drawn radius times the angle, and at 2.5 radians on a 0.2 m drum the rise reads 0.5 m

Every worked number matches the lesson: 4 m ÷ 2 m = 2 radians with slips 4 and 0.5; 1 radian on both circles; 2π = 6.28 with 0.28 over six rods, π = 3.14 and 57.3°; a quarter 1.57 with slips 1 and 0.25; 60° = 1.047 radians and 2 radians = 114.6°; 10 radians 1.59 turns to 213.0°, cos 10 = −0.839 and cos 10° = 0.985; 45° = 0.785 with slips 2578.3 and 0.25; 0.2 × 2.5 = 0.5 m; 0.524 m with slips 30 m and 0.262, and an edge of 3.14 m; 41.9 rad/s and 16.76 MW; sin 0.5 = 0.479 with slips 0.0087 and 0.5; 157.1 rad/s with slips 25 and 9,425; 4.71 m with slips 0.75 m and 270 m

Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, every wrong answer has its own hint and its own red row of working, the answer appears once it is given, and before an answer nothing in the picture gives it away

No label sits on another label or a handle, or runs off the picture, on any screen in any state: puzzles answered right, wrong or with Why? open, the arm dragged to every angle on circles of every size, the drum turned to every angle
Every demonstration has finished within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; each answer and Why? has settled within 1.8 s
